column4: The section names the root ع ط و through يُعْطِيكَ in 93:5; 108:1 addresses the same Prophet with أَعْطَيْنَاكَ, making the Lord's gift explicit. The following ayah supplies the sacrificial response.

The section reads sacrifice as a response to what the Lord gives; after the gift in 108:1, this ayah commands فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَانْحَرْ. Its own contribution is the prayer and slaughter directed to the Lord.
The section links the divine gift to a sacrificial return. This ayah names the sacrificial camels الْبُدْنَ, says there is good in them, directs people to feed the needy, and ends with gratitude.
The section's dictionary form الهدي is an animal led to the Haram; this ayah says the هَدْي reaches its مَحِلّ, the destination that makes the animal's directed movement concrete.

The section's dictionary form الهدي names animals sent toward the Haram. This ayah protects الْهَدْي among the sacred rites and describes people approaching the Sacred House seeking bounty and approval from their Lord.
This ayah specifies a livestock offering هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ, an animal that must reach the Kaaba. It gives a concrete instance of the section's Harem-bound hedy.
This ayah groups الْهَدْيَ with the Sacred House, sacred month, and garlands as things made to uphold people's religious life; it shows the sent animal functioning as a sacred sign.
The section frames the animal as a God-given blessing that prompts a response. In the Hajj scene here, people mention God over the livestock He provided, then eat from it and feed the poor.
The section's hedy is an animal moving toward a destination; this ayah describes benefits from sacrificial animals until an appointed time, then their place at the Ancient House.
The section's hedy moves toward its destination; this ayah states that the offering was prevented from reaching its place. That interruption is the direct reversal of the animal's intended arrival.

This ayah bounds the section's reciprocal-sacrifice reading: the animals' flesh and blood do not reach God; taqwa does. The material offering matters as a rite, while the verse names what reaches God.

The section's animal is driven toward a sacred destination. This ayah depicts pilgrims arriving for Hajj on lean camels from distant passes; 22:28 continues with the livestock offering and feeding, completing the arrival scene.

The section places the animal's arrival at the Haram within a pilgrimage. This ayah continues the rite by naming vows and circumambulation of the Ancient House; its own contribution is the human completion of the sanctuary visit.

This ayah says honoring God's شعائر comes from taqwa of hearts; 22:33 next specifies the sacrificial animals and their place at the Ancient House. It frames the offering as a sacred sign whose outward honor rests on inward reverence.

The section's source dictionary root ن ع م names camels as well as blessing. This ayah uses بَهِيمَةِ الْأَنْعَامِ for livestock over which God's name is mentioned, making the animal branch of that root part of a rite.
The section's source dictionary root ن ع م names camels; this ayah explicitly names الْأَنْعَامِ as animals people ride. It supplies a Qur'anic scene for the animal branch of the section's root note.

The section names نعمة as the Lord's blessing and ends by commanding its narration. Here riders are told to remember نِعْمَةَ رَبِّكُمْ and praise the One who subjected the mount; 43:12 supplies the livestock being ridden.

The section develops a meeting between the gift root ع ط و and the guidance root ه د ي. Moses' reply joins them in أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ, presenting giving and guidance as successive acts.

The section reads sacrifice as something presented to the Lord in response to His gift. This ayah explicitly places وَنُسُكِي, “my sacrifice/rite,” alongside prayer and says they are for Allah, Lord of the worlds.
The section's reciprocal reading is that one answers what God has given with an offering to Him. This ayah states the parallel principle directly: do good as Allah has done good to you.

The section's dictionary root ن ع م names livestock as well as blessing. This ayah says God created الْأَنْعَامَ for warmth, benefits, and food, making the animal itself a provision received from God.
The section's source root ن ع م includes the animal sense; this ayah calls الْأَنْعَامِ a lesson and names drink, benefits, and food received from them, presenting livestock as a divine provision.

The section's dictionary form الأضحية ties ḍuḥā to the animal slaughtered on Eid. This ayah uses the same root in ضُحَاهَا for the sun's morning brightness, keeping the sacrifice-time word connected to its daylight sense.

The section's source root for ضحى links the morning to an Eid offering. This ayah says God darkened night and brought out its ضُحَى; it echoes the Surah 93 opening's day-and-night frame around the image's named morning.

The section's dictionary form الأضحية links ضحى to the Eid sacrifice. This ayah sets a gathering on the day of adornment at ضُحًى, a festival-day morning that makes the section's time association concrete.

The section centers on an animal presented at the Haram. In the adjacent pilgrimage rule, this ayah permits sea game but bars land game during ihram, completing 5:95's contrast between hunted game and livestock sent as an offering.

The section's hedy is directed toward the Haram; 48:25 says it was blocked from its destination. This ayah completes the interrupted pilgrimage scene by promising the believers entry into the Sacred Mosque in safety.

This is a parallel, not the same destination: the section reads the animal's movement toward the Haram as sacred direction, while the rider's travel formula begun in 43:13 ends with إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ, naming the human return to God.

The section pairs niʿma as blessing with h-d-y as guidance. This ayah portrays Abraham as grateful for God's favors and then guided to a straight path, bringing those two roots together in one account of divine favor and human response.

The section's gift root ʿaṭā becomes an offering in its reciprocal reading. This ayah contributes the person who gives and is mindful; 92:7 completes the sequence by promising that God will ease that person's way, reversing the section's order of divine giving followed by human response.

The section reads sacrifice as a return for what God has given. This ayah states a specific reciprocal movement: what people spend is replaced by God, the best provider. It presents that giving relation in the opposite direction, without naming sacrifice.

This ayah joins honoring Allah's sacred ordinances to livestock made lawful under stated limits. It gives the section's sacred animal a frame of sanctuary law before the surrounding passage describes the rites and sacrificial animals.

The section's dictionary note ties the ḍuḥā root to the Eid offering; here the same forenoon word marks a time when divine punishment may reach a town at play. This is only a contrast in the time's valence, since the ayah itself describes no sacrifice.

The section's secondary dictionary sense says hady can mean camels; this ayah names camels among livestock pairs. That anchors the animal sense only: the ayah itself debates animal restrictions and does not describe a Hady offering.
